job.system:
You are the AI assistant for the Coalition Against Deep-Sea Mining. Our staff use you for day-to-day work: research, writing, data, scheduling, and operations.

About us: The Coalition Against Deep-Sea Mining (CADM) is a nonprofit advocacy organization based in Washington, DC. We believe that the industrial mining of the deep seabed, meaning the large-scale extraction of minerals from the ocean floor, poses a serious risk of irreversible destruction to deep-ocean ecosystems, and that no one currently knows how to conduct it without such damage. Our goal is a legally binding prohibition on commercial deep-sea mining, first in the United States and then through an international treaty. We work through lobbying, grassroots organizing, and public education.

Current focus: Our top priority this fall is S. 2817, the Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act, which we strongly support. The Senate Commerce Committee will mark up the bill on Thursday, October 15.

You run in our internal chat app, which has no tools, browsing, or code execution, so work everything out directly in your reply. Staff rely on your work, so be accurate and thorough.
job.prompt:
Before next Thursday's markup, can you go through the bill text below and find every loophole, ambiguity, or drafting problem: anything that would let companies keep going, or that would make the bill hard to enforce or easy to challenge?

Please list each issue as a numbered item: cite the section, then explain the problem in one to three sentences.

---

S. 2817 — Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act
(text as amended by the manager's amendment of October 6, 2026)

SECTION 1. SHORT TITLE.
This Act may be cited as the "Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act".

SEC. 2. DEFINITIONS.
In this Act:
(1) COMMERCIAL DEEP SEABED MINING.—The term "commercial deep seabed mining" means—
  (A) the recovery of more than 10,000 metric tons per year of polymetallic nodules or other mineral resources from the seabed at depths greater than 200 meters by a single vessel; or
  (B) any activity that the Secretary determines poses risks to deep-sea ecosystems comparable to those of the activities described in subparagraph (A).
(2) U.S. PERSON.—The term "U.S. person" means a citizen of the United States or a corporation organized under the laws of a State.
(3) COVERED VESSEL.—The term "covered vessel" means a vessel of more than 5,000 gross tons equipped for the recovery of seabed mineral resources.

SEC. 3. PROHIBITION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—It shall be unlawful for any person in the United States, or any U.S. person anywhere, to engage in commercial deep seabed mining.
(b) EXISTING OPERATIONS.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to mining conducted under an exploration license issued before the date of enactment of this Act.
(c) ENVIRONMENTAL ASSESSMENT.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to activities conducted for the purpose of environmental assessment.

SEC. 4. REGISTRY.
(a) REGISTRATION.—The operator of each covered vessel shall register the vessel with the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.
(b) REPORTS.—Each registered operator shall submit to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration a quarterly report, certified by the operator, describing the recovery activities conducted by the vessel.

SEC. 5. PENALTIES.
(a) CIVIL PENALTY.—Any person who violates section 3 shall be liable for a civil penalty of not more than $1,000,000 for each day on which the violation occurs, for any violation occurring on or after the date of enactment of this Act.
(b) CRIMINAL PENALTY.—Any person who willfully violates section 3 shall be fined under title 18, United States Code, imprisoned for not more than 10 years, or both.

SEC. 6. INTERNATIONAL AGREEMENT.
The Secretary of State shall seek to negotiate, not later than 18 months after the date of enactment of this Act, an international agreement establishing prohibitions equivalent to those in section 3.

SEC. 7. DURATION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—The prohibition in section 3 shall remain in effect until Congress, acting on a report of the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, finds by joint resolution that commercial deep seabed mining can be conducted without serious harm.
(b) SUNSET.—This Act shall cease to have effect on the date that is 10 years after the date of enactment of this Act.

SEC. 8. EFFECTIVE DATE.
This Act shall take effect 180 days after the date of enactment.

---

result:
I read the manager's amendment text as written. Items are in section order, with cross-cutting problems at the end. The most serious are 1, 6, 12-13, 19, 22, 24, 25 and 27. A few items depend on how the bill interacts with existing law, such as the Deep Seabed Hard Mineral Resources Act (DSHMRA) and the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act (OCSLA), so please have counsel or CRS confirm those before they go into talking points.

**Sec. 2: Definitions**

1. **Sec. 2(1)(A), volume threshold.** The bill reaches only recovery above 10,000 metric tons per year. Anything below that, including pilot-scale or "test" mining, is lawful. The definition also turns on tonnage rather than commercial purpose, so a company selling material from sub-threshold operations is unaffected.
2. **Sec. 2(1)(A), "single vessel."** The threshold applies per vessel, with no aggregation across vessels, affiliates, or a common operator. A company could split recovery among several vessels, or use shuttle and collector vessels, and stay under the line.
3. **Sec. 2(1)(A), "per year."** It is unclear whether this is a calendar-year total or an annualized rate. A 3-month campaign extracting 40,000 tons arguably isn't "more than 10,000 tons per year." The bill also doesn't say whether tons are wet or dry, or who measures them.
4. **Sec. 2(1)(A), "recovery" and "mineral resources."** Neither term is defined. Seafloor massive sulfides, cobalt crusts, and sediments may not be clearly covered. The bill also doesn't address seabed disturbance, in-situ processing, or discharge that isn't "recovery."
5. **Sec. 2(1)(A), 200-meter depth and geography.** The bill doesn't say whether it reaches the U.S. EEZ and outer continental shelf, where OCSLA governs minerals, or only areas beyond national jurisdiction. Operations at or above 200 meters are outside the definition entirely.
6. **Sec. 2(1)(B), Secretary's determination.** "The Secretary" is never defined in the bill, and Sec. 6 separately names the Secretary of State. The determination is discretionary, has no deadline or criteria beyond "comparable" risk, and nothing compels the Secretary to act. Because criminal liability under Sec. 5(b) could hinge on it, it also invites fair-notice, vagueness, and delegation challenges.
7. **Sec. 2(2), "U.S. person."** The definition covers only citizens and corporations organized under State law. It leaves out foreign-incorporated subsidiaries of U.S. companies, partnerships and other non-corporate entities, lawful permanent residents, and entities organized in D.C. or the territories, which are not "States." There is no ownership or control test.
8. **Sec. 2(3), "covered vessel."** Vessels of 5,000 gross tons or less are exempt from the registry, and "equipped for the recovery" is vague (modular or temporary equipment, for example). The term appears only in Sec. 4, so it does no work in the prohibition itself.

**Sec. 3: Prohibition**

9. **Sec. 3(a), jurisdictional reach.** "In the United States" is undefined (territorial sea? EEZ? U.S.-flagged vessels at sea?). Foreign persons operating abroad, including on foreign-flagged vessels, are outside the prohibition even if they sell into the U.S. market.
10. **Sec. 3(a), conduct covered.** The bill bars only "engaging in" mining. It doesn't bar processing, importing, selling, financing, insuring, or providing port and supply services for seabed minerals, and it has no aiding-and-abetting language.
11. **Sec. 3(a), existing law.** The bill doesn't amend or repeal DSHMRA or OCSLA, or bar NOAA or Interior from issuing licenses and permits. A company holding a federal permit could argue the permit authorizes its activity. Agencies could also keep processing applications in the interim.
12. **Sec. 3(b), grandfathering scope.** The exemption for "mining conducted under" pre-enactment exploration licenses has no cap, no time limit, and no limit on scope. It doesn't address renewals, extensions, modifications, or transfers. It also blurs exploration and commercial recovery, since exploration licenses ordinarily don't authorize commercial recovery, which invites litigation over what is covered.
13. **Sec. 3(b), "exploration license" undefined.** The term could include foreign-issued or International Seabed Authority-sponsored licenses held by U.S. persons, or pending applications. Because the cutoff is the date of enactment, there is also an incentive to rush licenses through before then.
14. **Sec. 3(c), environmental assessment exemption.** The exemption turns on subjective "purpose," with no definition of environmental assessment, no volume cap, no permit or review, and no requirement that data be made public. It is an obvious route for pretextual bulk sampling or test mining.

**Sec. 4: Registry**

15. **Sec. 4(a), registration.** There is no deadline for registering, no definition of "operator," and no tie between registration and the Sec. 3 prohibition. NOAA also has no stated authority to refuse or revoke registration.
16. **Sec. 4(b), reports.** The bill doesn't say what a report must contain, how it is verified, or whether it is public. It relies on self-certification, with no audit, inspection, or vessel-tracking requirement. Nothing says the reports are available to the public or to other agencies.
17. **Sec. 4, no consequence for violations.** Sec. 5 penalizes only violations of Sec. 3, so failing to register or report, or filing false reports, has no stated penalty. General false-statement statutes might apply, but the bill doesn't say so.

**Sec. 5: Penalties and enforcement**

18. **Sec. 5(a), timing conflict.** The civil penalty applies to violations "on or after the date of enactment," but Sec. 8 delays the Act's effect by 180 days. That leaves it unclear whether conduct in the gap is penalized, and it invites a fair-notice defense.
19. **Sec. 5, no enforcement machinery.** The bill designates no enforcing agency and gives no authority for inspections, boarding, subpoenas, seizure, or injunctions. It also has no rulemaking authority, no forfeiture of vessels, minerals, or proceeds, and no procedures for assessing penalties (notice, hearing, factors). The $1,000,000 cap is also not inflation-indexed.
20. **Sec. 5(a), "each day."** It isn't clear how days are counted for intermittent or continuing operations, or how a violation is proven day by day without a reporting or monitoring requirement.
21. **Sec. 5(b), "willfully."** The mens rea is demanding, and defendants may argue they didn't know the conduct was unlawful or exempt. There is no lower "knowing" tier, no organizational or officer liability language, and no express extraterritorial criminal jurisdiction for U.S. persons abroad.
22. **No citizen-suit or judicial-review provision.** Enforcement depends entirely on executive discretion. A future administration that is hostile or simply under-resourced could decline to enforce, and outside groups would have no clear route to compel it.

**Sec. 6: International agreement**

23. **Sec. 6, hortatory and ambiguous.** "Seek to negotiate, not later than 18 months" could mean the deadline is for starting talks or for concluding an agreement. There is no reporting requirement, no consequence for missing it, and no definition of "equivalent." There is also no forum named (the U.S. is not a party to UNCLOS) and no leverage such as trade measures.

**Sec. 7: Duration**

24. **Sec. 7(a), lifting standard.** "Serious harm" is undefined. The bill doesn't say who requests the National Academies report, when, with what funding, or on what scope. It also doesn't say whether a joint resolution lifts the prohibition entirely or only for specified activities.
25. **Sec. 7(a) vs. 7(b), internal contradiction.** Subsection (a) keeps the prohibition in place until Congress finds otherwise, but (b) ends the Act automatically after 10 years whatever the science says. This is the most consequential flaw, because industry can simply wait out the clock and plan around the sunset date.
26. **Sec. 7(b), no savings clause.** Nothing preserves enforcement of violations committed before the sunset, or pending actions. Since Sec. 8 delays effect by 180 days, the prohibition would be operative for only about 9.5 years.

**Sec. 8: Effective date**

27. **Sec. 8, 180-day window.** Combined with the Sec. 3(b) grandfathering and no cutoff for new activity, the gap invites companies to rush permits, begin operations, and claim vested rights. Nothing imposes an interim bar on issuing new licenses or starting new operations.

**Cross-cutting**

28. **No findings or purpose section.** The bill states no findings, no purpose, and no constitutional basis (commerce power, extraterritorial reach). That weakens its defense in court. After *Loper Bright*, courts won't defer to agency readings of ambiguous text, so every gap above will be resolved by judges, not NOAA.
29. **No severability clause.** If a court strikes one provision, such as the extraterritorial reach or the Secretary's discretionary determination, the rest of the Act could be put at risk.
30. **No appropriation or funding authorization.** NOAA gets new registry and reporting duties and no resources to carry them out.
31. **Takings exposure.** The bill doesn't address holders of pending applications, DSHMRA permits, or other claimed vested interests. Without a transition or compensation approach, it invites Fifth Amendment litigation, which opponents will use to delay or enjoin enforcement.

I can turn this into a markup memo with proposed amendment language for the highest-priority items, or a one-page version for Hill staff. Which would be more useful before Thursday?
